It recounts that Arthur Evans purchased and published the ring, despite an archaeological board in Athens having declined to buy it because its members considered it a modern forgery. Evans interpreted the imagery on the bezel as a Minoan representation of the afterlife, including a human couple entering the Elysian Fields. This paper describes the Archer Fragment, a two-piece wall-painting fragment from the Palace of Nestor at Pylos, rather than a "Ring of Nestor." The fragment, found during the 1939 excavation and later stored in the Chora Museum, preserves part of a white-skinned human figure against a bright blue ground, including an arm, a short blue sleeve, wrist bands or bracelets, and an object interpreted as a bow. The authors reconstruct the excavated context, condition, iconography, and painting technique of the fragment. They report that the fragment had been removed from the palace walls before its final destruction, was probably broken in antiquity, and shows no obvious burning or moisture-related degradation. The paper also discusses alternative interpretations of the figure's pose, arm orientation, and some painted details. Scientific analyses of the pigments and binders are presented in the paper, whose abstract states that Egyptian blue was extensively used and that egg served as a binder in a tempera rather than fresco technique.
